rows.title: Policy divergence
rows.figure: Blackout: Oct hold 84-87%; Dec hike ~89.5% (Oct-15 vintage); BoC Oct odds 25-32%
rows.read: Most central banks are holding in October and lining up for December, so the story is who raises rates first. The Bank of England and Bank of Japan look closest to hiking, which tends to pull money toward the pound and yen; the Fed, ECB and Bank of Canada are waiting on data, and Canada's inflation today is the swing factor.

rows.title: Growth differentials
rows.figure: China Q3 GDP 4.5% beat (retail +1.1% standout); today: Canada CPI + BoC survey
rows.read: China grew a little faster than expected, mostly because shoppers spent more, which is good news for countries that sell to China, like Australia. Elsewhere growth is steady but uneven, so this week inflation matters more for currencies than growth does.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: US hot week stands; Canada CPI today; UK CPI 3.4% fc Wed; NZ CPI 3.8% fc Wed
rows.read: Prices are still rising too fast almost everywhere: US inflation came in hot three times last week and Europe's is at a three-year high, with expensive oil feeding it. That keeps central banks under pressure to hold rates high or raise them, and this week's UK, New Zealand and Japan readings decide how much.

rows.title: Risk sentiment
rows.figure: No retaliation yet, talks stalled — haven bid sheathed at Monday's open; France unrest hits the euro
rows.read: The weekend's big fears, a Middle East flare-up or a surprise Iran deal, didn't happen, so markets stayed calm and the safe-haven currencies (yen, franc, dollar) got no extra lift. The stress point moved to France, where violent protests are weighing on the euro.

rows.title: Terms of trade / commodities
rows.figure: Brent ~$108 (-1 to -1.8%), WTI ~$101 held; spread ~$7.5-8 — tanker-risk premium ~2x normal
rows.read: Oil is still expensive, near $108–110, because shipping in the Gulf and Russian supply are both at risk. That helps oil exporters like Canada and hurts importers like Japan and the eurozone, and New Zealand's widening trade gap is a small drag on its dollar.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: No new COT until Friday; funds long AUD (79th pctile) — the pain trade is down
rows.read: Speculators aren't heavily leaned in most currencies, so there's little risk of a sudden rush for the exits. The exception is the Australian dollar: hedge funds already hold a lot of bets that it rises, so if the news turns it has the most room to fall.

rows.title: Fiscal & sovereign risk
rows.figure: FY26 $1.992T; Graham waiver stands (backlash, no reversal); France: vote Tue, Moody's Fri
rows.read: Government finances are a slow-burning worry: the US deficit is the biggest in five years, and France's budget fight is making investors demand more to hold its debt. France is the one to watch this week, with a budget vote Tuesday and Moody's rating review Friday that can move the euro.
